Appendix A Templated Radix Tree Construction

The templated radix tree (TRT) is built from the optimized workflow DAG to capture the shared prefix structure and data dependencies among all LLM operators. The construction process, outlined in Algorithm 2, translates the operator-level graph into the TRT’s prefix-based representation.

First, we perform a topological sort of the workflow’s operators to ensure that an operator’s dependencies are processed before the operator itself (Line 6). The algorithm then iterates through the sorted operators (Line 7). For each LLM operator, it constructs a prefix template, a sequence of static tokens and dynamic placeholders that represent inputs from antecedent operators (Line 9). This template is generated by recursively traversing the operator’s inputs within the DAG: static strings are appended directly, while dependencies on other operators are encoded as placeholders.

With the prefix template and its set of LLM dependencies identified (Line 8), the operator is inserted into the TRT (Line 10). The tree.add method implements standard radix tree insertion, traversing from the root to find the longest common prefix. If the template diverges from an existing path, the relevant node is split to create a new branch. The LLM operator is then added as a new leaf node. Its dependencies on other LLM operators are recorded as directed edges that connect it to the corresponding leaf nodes retrieved from the node_map. This map maintains the correspondence between operator IDs and their nodes in the TRT, ensuring that dependencies are correctly resolved as the tree is built (Line 13).

The time complexity of this procedure is determined by the initial graph traversal and the subsequent insertion of each LLM operator into the tree. Let NN be the number of operators and |E||E| be the number of dependency edges in the workflow DAG. The topological sort takes O⁡(N+|E|)O(N+|E|) time. The total work to generate all prefix templates is also bounded by O⁡(N+|E|)O(N+|E|), as it involves traversing the DAG. Let Nl​l​m≤NN_{llm}\leq N be the number of LLM operators and LL be the maximum length of a prefix template. Inserting one template takes O⁡(L)O(L) time. The total complexity is therefore O⁡(N+|E|+Nl​l​m⋅L)O(N+|E|+N_{llm}\cdot L). In a connected DAG, |E||E| is at least N−1N-1, so the complexity simplifies to O⁡(|E|+Nl​l​m⋅L)O(|E|+N_{llm}\cdot L).

Appendix B Complexity Analysis of the Scheduling Algorithm

In this section, we provide a formal proof for the time complexity of our cache-aware scheduling algorithm, as detailed in Algorithm 1. We demonstrate that the algorithm has a polynomial time complexity in the size of the TRT and the dependency graph.

Definitions Let T=(V,E)T=(V,E) be the input TRT, where |V||V| is the number of nodes. Let L⊂VL\subset V be the set of leaf nodes, which represent the LLM operators to be scheduled. The dependencies among these operators are given by the DAG G=(L,E′)G=(L,E^{\prime}), where |E′||E^{\prime}| is the number of dependency edges. Let |Vi​n​t|=|V|−|L|−1|V_{int}|=|V|-|L|-1 be the number of internal nodes in TT, let d=depth​(T)d=\text{depth}(T) be the maximum depth of the TRT, and let cm​a​xc_{max} be the maximum branching factor (i.e., number of children) of any node in TT.

Proof of Complexity

Theorem B.1.

The time complexity of the scheduling algorithm (Algorithm 1) is O⁡(|Vi​n​t|⋅cm​a​x3+|E′|⋅d)O(|V_{int}|\cdot c_{max}^{3}+|E^{\prime}|\cdot d).

Proof.

The algorithm consists of two primary phases: an initialization phase and a recursive scheduling phase. We analyze the complexity of each phase separately.

1. Initialization Phase: The initialization phase constructs the internal scheduling tree data structure from the input TRT and the dependency graph GG. This involves three main steps:

  1. (1)

    Traversing the TRT (TT) to create corresponding scheduling nodes, which takes O⁡(|V|)O(|V|) time.

  2. (2)

    Processing the dependency graph G=(L,E′)G=(L,E^{\prime}) to compute the depth of each LLM operator (leaf node). This is equivalent to a topological sort on GG, which costs O⁡(|L|+|E′|)O(|L|+|E^{\prime}|).

  3. (3)

    Building the sibling dependency maps by performing a post-order traversal of the TRT. During this traversal, each dependency in E′E^{\prime} is examined to determine if it is internal to a subtree or connects sibling subtrees. This step has a complexity of O⁡(|V|+|E′|)O(|V|+|E^{\prime}|).

Therefore, the time complexity of the initialization phase is dominated by the tree and graph traversals, resulting in O⁡(|V|+|E′|)O(|V|+|E^{\prime}|).

2. Recursive Scheduling Phase: The core of the algorithm lies in the Schedule function, which invokes the recursive function Recurse. The complexity is dominated by the work done within all calls to Recurse. We analyze the work done at a single internal node u∈Vi​n​tu\in V_{int}. The work at an internal node uu is driven by the while loop that iterates until all of its children are scheduled. Let cuc_{u} be the number of children of node uu. The loop runs at most cuc_{u} times. Within each iteration, the most computationally intensive operations are SelectBestChild and the subsequent state updates.

  • •

    Cost of SelectBestChild: This function implements our cost-based heuristic. To determine the optimal child to schedule next (based on progress and readiness), the function must analyze the inter-dependencies among the currently unscheduled sibling subtrees. This requires constructing a temporary dependency graph among the kk remaining children and analyzing its structure (e.g., by finding strongly connected components to determine topological depth). Such an analysis has a complexity of at least O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}). The total work for the while loop at node uu is therefore the sum of this cost over its iterations:

    ∑k=1cuO⁡(k2)=O⁡(cu3)\sum_{k=1}^{c_{u}}O(k^{2})=O(c_{u}^{3})

    Summing this cost over all internal nodes in the tree gives the first term of our complexity: O⁡(|Vi​n​t|⋅cm​a​x3)O(|V_{int}|\cdot c_{max}^{3}).

  • •

    Cost of State Updates: After scheduling a child, the UpdateState function is called on the remaining sibling children. This propagates the effects of newly resolved dependencies. Over the entire execution of the algorithm, a single dependency edge in E′E^{\prime} may be re-evaluated each time a scheduling decision is made that could affect its status. The maximum number of times an edge can be re-evaluated is proportional to its depth in the TRT, which is bounded by dd. Therefore, the total cumulative work for all state updates across the entire algorithm is bounded by O⁡(|E′|⋅d)O(|E^{\prime}|\cdot d).

Combining the costs from the initialization and scheduling phases, the dominant factor is the recursive scheduling phase. The total time complexity is the sum of the costs of iterative child selection and cumulative state updates.

O⁡(|V|+|E′|)+O⁡(|Vi​n​t|⋅cm​a​x3+|E′|⋅d)O(|V|+|E^{\prime}|)+O(|V_{int}|\cdot c_{max}^{3}+|E^{\prime}|\cdot d)

As |V||V| and |E′||E^{\prime}| are subsumed by the terms in the scheduling phase for any non-trivial workflow, the final complexity is O⁡(|Vi​n​t|⋅cm​a​x3+|E′|⋅d)O(|V_{int}|\cdot c_{max}^{3}+|E^{\prime}|\cdot d). ∎

Appendix C Agentic Workflows DSL

Helium’s DSL allows users to define agentic workflows using a concise set of primitive operators, listed in Table 6. Designed as a lazy, symbolic dataflow system, the DSL separates workflow definition from execution.

  • •

    IO Operators: Input and Output define the workflow’s interface, allowing batches of data to be injected and results to be retrieved. Data nodes encapsulate static batch data embedded directly within the workflow DAG.

  • •

    Prompt Operators: Format handles string interpolation for prompt templating, while Lambda allows users to inject arbitrary Python code for stateless transformations (e.g., parsing LLM outputs).

  • •

    Model Operators: The LLM operator encapsulates calls to the inference engine. It accepts formatted prompts and conversation history, returning generated responses that flow to downstream operators.

By composing these primitives, users build a symbolic DAG that the Helium runtime analyzes to perform global optimizations like proactive caching and cache-aware scheduling.

Appendix D Prefix Cache Utilization

In this section, we describe additional prefix cache utilization results following our end-to-end benchmark. We evaluate Helium and the baselines on the Trading workflow with a batch size of 16 using the Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B models. The results are summarized in Table 7.

Overall, Helium achieves the highest prefix cache hit rates for Qwen3-8B across all baselines, and is competitive for Qwen3-14B. For Qwen3-8B, Helium outperforms all baselines by 27.5% to 37.3%. The largest gains are over LangGraph (37.3%) and KVFlow (33.9%), both of which lack the global scheduling awareness to align requests with shared prefixes. OpWise achieves even lower hit rate than vLLM for Qwen3-8B, as the Trading workflow exhibits more prefix sharing across operators (e.g., system prompts shared across agents) than across queries, making operator-by-operator execution especially harmful for cache reuse.

For Qwen3-14B, Helium’s advantage is more modest (up to 14.9%), and vLLM achieves a marginally higher hit rate (+0.3%) than Helium. The larger KV cache footprint of Qwen3-14B increases memory pressure, which limits Helium’s ability to retain all precomputed prefixes and reduces the effectiveness of proactive caching relative to the smaller model. Importantly, however, vLLM’s competitive hit rate does not translate into competitive end-to-end latency: as shown in Section 7.2, vLLM incurs extremely high latency because it executes each query’s operators sequentially, foregoing the batch computation that Helium’s scheduler exploits. This confirms that a high cache hit rate alone is insufficient: global workflow-aware scheduling is essential to translate cache reuse into end-to-end performance gains.

Parrot trails Helium by 29.4% for Qwen3-8B. Although Parrot dispatches requests sharing the same prefix to the same engine to maximize cache hits, its routing heuristic creates severe load imbalance across workers. This congestion increases memory pressure on overloaded engines, triggering more frequent KV cache evictions that paradoxically reduce cache hit rates. The result is that Parrot’s strategy undermines its own prefix-reuse objective, leading to both lower hit rates and significantly higher end-to-end latency as shown in Section 7.2. These results collectively highlight the advantage of Helium’s cost-based, globally-aware approach to cache-aware scheduling.
